title: Motion of Satellite
short_intro: The motion of a satellite around a central body is governed by universal gravitation acting as a centripetal force. It describes the orbital mechanics of natural and artificial satellites under conservative central force fields.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Orbital velocity, time period of satellites, height of geostationary satellites, and total energy of a satellite in circular orbit.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Elliptical orbits, areal velocity conservation (Kepler's second law), angular momentum conservation, escape velocity, and orbital perturbations.

concept_notes.heading: Orbital Velocity and Height
bullets: The orbital velocity of a satellite depends on the mass of the central body and the radius of the orbit, but is independent of the mass of the satellite.
For a satellite revolving close to the Earth's surface, the orbital velocity is approximately 7.9 km/s.
As the orbital radius increases, the orbital velocity decreases while the potential energy increases.

concept_notes.heading: Time Period and Geostationary Orbit
bullets: The square of the time period of a satellite is directly proportional to the cube of its orbital radius (Kepler's Third Law).
A geostationary satellite rotates in the equatorial plane with a time period of exactly 24 hours, matching the Earth's rotational period.
The height of a geostationary satellite is approximately 35,800 km above the Earth's surface.

concept_notes.heading: Energy of an Orbiting Satellite
bullets: The total mechanical energy of a bound satellite is negative, indicating a bound system under an attractive central force.
Kinetic energy is equal in magnitude to half of the potential energy and negative of the total energy.
Binding energy is defined as the negative of the total mechanical energy required to remove the satellite to infinity.

concept_notes.heading: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
bullets: First Law (Law of Orbits): Every satellite moves in an elliptical orbit with the central body at one of the foci.
Second Law (Law of Areas): The position vector of the satellite sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time, reflecting conservation of angular momentum.
Third Law (Law of Periods): The square of the time period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis.

derivations.title: Orbital Velocity and Time Period of a Satellite
derivations.conditions: Circular orbit of radius r = R + h around a spherical Earth of mass M and radius R.
steps: Equate the gravitational force to the required centripetal force: \frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv_0^2}{r}
Express time period T as distance over orbital speed: T = \frac{2\pi r}{v_0} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}

derivations.title: Total Energy of a Satellite in Circular Orbit
derivations.conditions: Satellite of mass m in a circular orbit of radius r around mass M.
steps: Write kinetic energy from centripetal condition \frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{GMm}{r^2}: K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{GMm}{2r}
Sum kinetic and potential energy for total mechanical energy E: E = K + U = \frac{GMm}{2r} - \frac{GMm}{r} = -\frac{GMm}{2r}

graphs_and_experiments.title: Potential, Kinetic, and Total Energy vs. Orbital Radius
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Plot of U (negative hyperbola), K (positive hyperbola), and E (negative hyperbola below U) as a function of r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that total energy is negative (bound state) and kinetic energy is half the magnitude of potential energy.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct identification of energy curves and bound system conditions in multiple-choice questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Square of Time Period vs. Cube of Orbital Radius (T^2 vs. r^3)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin with slope 4π^2 / (GM).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Verifies Kepler's Third Law, confirming the inverse-square nature of gravitational force.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting slope values to calculate central mass M.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Orbital Velocity vs. Orbital Radius
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A decaying curve representing inverse square root dependence v proportional to 1 / sqrt(r).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that satellites closer to the central body travel faster than those farther away.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions comparing speeds of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and Geostationary satellites.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the orbital velocity of an artificial satellite revolving in a circular orbit at a height of 600 km above the Earth's surface. (Take R = 6400 km, g = 9.8 m/s^2)
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: R = 6400 km = 6.4 \times 10^6 m, h = 600 km = 0.6 \times 10^6 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2.
Calculate orbital radius r = R + h = 6.4 \times 10^6 + 0.6 \times 10^6 = 7.0 \times 10^6 m.
Use formula v_0 = \sqrt{gR^2 / r} or v_0 = \sqrt{GM / r} where GM = gR^2.

solved_numericals.question: A satellite of mass 200 kg is revolving in a circular orbit of radius 2R around the Earth. Find its kinetic energy, potential energy, and total energy. (Take R = 6400 km, g = 9.8 m/s^2)
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: m = 200 kg, r = 2R = 2 \times 6.4 \times 10^6 m = 1.28 \times 10^7 m, GM = gR^2.
Calculate Potential Energy U = -GMm / r = -gR^2 m / (2R) = -gRm / 2.
Substitute numerical values for U: U = - (9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6 \times 200) / 2 = -6.272 \times 10^9 J.
Calculate Total Energy E = K + U = -3.136 \times 10^9 J.

solved_numericals.question: Find the minimum energy required to launch a satellite of mass 1000 kg from the Earth's surface into a circular orbit at an altitude equal to the Earth's radius R.
solution_steps: Initial energy of the satellite on Earth's surface: E_i = K_i + U_i = 0 - \frac{GMm}{R} = -\frac{GMm}{R}.
Final total energy in circular orbit at r = R + R = 2R: E_f = -\frac{GMm}{2(2R)} = -\frac{GMm}{4R}.

assumptions_and_limitations: The central body is assumed to be spherically symmetric with a uniform mass distribution.
Atmospheric drag and dissipative frictional forces are neglected unless explicitly stated.
Gravitational perturbations from the Sun, Moon, and non-spherical Earth oblateness (J2 term) are ignored in basic circular orbit models.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A satellite in orbit is beyond the Earth's gravitational pull, which is why astronauts float.
common_misconceptions.correct: Gravity is very much present; astronauts float because both the satellite and the astronauts are in free fall together towards the Earth.
common_misconceptions.why: Centripetal acceleration equals local acceleration due to gravity, producing apparent weightlessness.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A heavier satellite requires a higher orbital velocity to stay in the same orbit.
common_misconceptions.correct: Orbital velocity is independent of the mass of the satellite.
common_misconceptions.why: Mass cancels out when equating gravitational force and centripetal force.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Total energy of a satellite can be positive.
common_misconceptions.correct: Total energy of a bound satellite is always negative.
common_misconceptions.why: A positive total energy implies an unbound hyperbolic or parabolic trajectory, not a closed orbit.

quick_revision: Orbital velocity varies inversely as the square root of the orbital radius.
